hero.name: Dev
hero.who: a pharmacy owner in Dehradun who has meant to write a novel for fifteen years

story.b: Dev runs a small pharmacy near the clock tower in Dehradun. In the bottom drawer of the counter lies a notebook with the title of his novel on the cover, a story about the hill village where he grew up. He has meant to write it since he was twenty-five. He is forty now. Every few months he sits down to start, and something happens. A sudden headache. An urgent stock order. A cricket match he must watch. Or he decides he should read more novels first, to be ready. His wife has stopped asking about the book. His son once found the notebook and asked why it had only four pages. Dev laughed, but that night he could not sleep.

ask.q: Dev keeps finding reasons not to start his novel. What should he understand first?
o: He is just lazy and needs to feel guilty enough to start
Something pushes back every time he begins, and it can be named and beaten
He is not ready yet and should read many more novels first
ask.why: Calling himself lazy adds guilt but explains nothing, and preparing forever is one of the ways delay disguises itself. Seeing the headaches, sudden errands and endless preparation as one force that appears whenever he starts helps him spot it and push through.

chapters.take: The urge to delay is not a character flaw. It is a force you can recognise.

story.b: Dev decides to watch for the force that stops him, and he gives it a name: resistance. On Sunday morning he sits at the dining table with the notebook. Within five minutes he wants to reorganise the spice rack. Then he feels sleepy. Then he must reply in the local chemists' WhatsApp group. Then he thinks he will start properly next Sunday, after the tax filing. This time each urge gets a tick in the margin, with a word beside it: tidying, sleepy, phone, next week. By noon there are eleven ticks and two paragraphs. It is not much. But looking at the ticks, Dev understands it was never about time. Something shows up every single time he tries.

ask.q: The next Sunday, Dev suddenly feels he must sort old bills before writing. What should he do?
o: Notice the urge as resistance and write fifteen minutes before anything else
Sort the bills first, since a clear desk will help him write better
Skip writing today and wait for a morning with no distractions
ask.why: The urge to sort bills arrives exactly when the writing is about to begin, which is resistance in disguise. A distraction-free morning never comes. Naming the urge and writing first, even briefly, takes away its power over him.

chapters.take: Name the excuses that appear when you start. They are usually resistance in disguise.

story.b: Dev notices something odd. He has no trouble writing the monthly newsletter for his pharmacy customers. He finishes it in twenty minutes, all monsoon reminders and new stock. Nothing stops him. But the moment he opens the novel, especially the chapter where his boyhood self leaves the village for the plains, his chest tightens. He realises the resistance is strongest around the thing he cares about most. The newsletter does not matter enough to scare him. The novel does. So he flips his thinking. The dread is not a sign to stop. It is a sign pointing at the work that matters. That evening Dev writes the first page of the leaving chapter, for fifteen shaky minutes.

ask.q: Dev's cousin Pema dreams of starting a homestay but feels sick with fear, while planning a picnic feels easy. What might that fear mean?
o: The homestay is probably a bad idea, since it makes her so uneasy
The fear may be pointing at the work that matters most to her
She should stick to easy plans until the fear fades on its own
ask.why: Fear does not always mean danger. It is often strongest around the work we care about most, which is why a picnic feels easy and a dream feels scary. Waiting for the fear to vanish usually means waiting forever. Starting small despite it is the way forward.

chapters.take: The work you dread most is often the work that matters most to you.

story.b: Dev thinks about his pharmacy. He opens the shutter at nine every morning, whether he feels like it or not. In fever season, in the rain, the day after his cousin's wedding. He never waits for inspiration to sell cough syrup. Yet with the novel he has behaved like an amateur, waiting for the right mood. So he makes a decision about attitude. From now on, writing is a job with fixed hours: 6:00 to 6:45 every morning at the dining table, before the house wakes. Some mornings the words are flat and boring. Dev writes anyway, and he stops at 6:45 sharp. After three weeks he has written more than in the past fifteen years.

ask.q: Dev wakes up tired and uninspired one morning. What would a professional attitude say?
o: Skip today and write twice as much when inspiration returns
Read writing tips online until he feels motivated again
Show up at the usual time and write, even if the words are plain
ask.why: Waiting for inspiration is how fifteen years slipped by, and reading tips feels like work while avoiding it. A professional shows up at the fixed time whatever the mood. Plain words can be fixed later, but words never written cannot.

chapters.take: Amateurs wait for the mood. Professionals show up at the same time anyway.

story.h: Four likes and a spelling mistake
story.b: Excited, Dev posts his first chapter in an online writers' group. He checks his phone between customers all day. By night it has four likes and one comment pointing out a spelling mistake. He feels crushed. For three mornings the alarm rings at six and he lies in bed thinking nobody cares. On the fourth morning he sees what has happened. He has handed his writing to strangers' thumbs. If likes decide whether he writes, he is no longer in charge. So Dev goes back to the dining table and makes a rule. The novel is his own private workshop, a place he returns to for its own sake. He will share it someday, but praise will be a bonus, never the reason.

ask.q: Dev's son posts his drawings online and wants to quit when they get few likes. What is the best advice?
o: Draw for the joy of drawing, and treat likes as a small bonus
Post more often and use popular hashtags to get more likes
Stop posting and stop drawing, since nobody seems interested
ask.why: If likes decide whether he keeps drawing, strangers control his craft. Chasing hashtags ties him even tighter to approval, and quitting lets a few numbers end something he loves. Drawing for its own sake keeps the craft his, and any praise becomes a happy extra.

chapters.take: Do the work for its own sake. Praise is a bonus, never the fuel.

story.b: Halfway through the novel, Dev hits a wall. He does not know what happens after the boy reaches the plains. For a week he waits for an idea before sitting down. Nothing arrives. Then, on Monday, he sits at 6:00 anyway and simply describes the boy's first morning in the new town. Somewhere on the second page, he remembers the smell of the bakery near his old hostel and a night watchman who used to tell stories by a small fire. Suddenly the middle of the book has a character. Later that week, a retired teacher who buys her tablets at his counter mentions she runs a small writers' circle on Saturdays. Dev cannot explain it. He only knows it started after he sat down.

ask.q: Dev's friend says he will start writing songs once inspiration strikes. What would Dev tell him?
o: Wait for the right mood, because forced songs are never any good
Sit down to write before he feels ready, since ideas tend to come during the work
Collect song ideas in his head for a year before writing any
ask.why: Waiting for the mood or collecting ideas for a year both put the work off, often forever. Inspiration usually shows up after you begin, not before. Sitting down is the one part he controls, and once he does, ideas and help tend to follow.

chapters.take: Inspiration usually shows up during the work, so sit down first.

story.b: Eight weeks later, Dev reads a chapter aloud at the retired teacher's Saturday circle, in a small room above a stationery shop. His hands shake a little, but his voice holds. The notebook from the drawer is full, and there is a second one now. Nothing magical happened. He still feels resistance most mornings, as a sudden urge to check stock or tidy the table. He just recognises it, ticks the margin and keeps writing from 6:00 to 6:45. The pharmacy opens at nine as always. The novel is not finished, and the online group still gives him few likes. But his son now asks each evening how many pages, and Dev always has an answer.

chapters.take: The work gets done by showing up daily, not by waiting to feel ready.
